summary: Describes the vacation extension to Sieve, an autoresponder like the Unix vacation command. It includes safety features to avoid problems such as message loops. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This is an automatic reply that says I am away. It has safeguards so two auto-replies do not keep answering each other forever.

questions: what is the sieve vacation extension
how does sieve vacation avoid mail loops
what does the vacation days parameter do
subtitle: How a Sieve mail filter can send an automatic 'I am away' reply without starting mail loops or spamming people.

tldr.problem: Users who are away want incoming mail answered automatically, but naive autoresponders can reply to mailing lists, to other robots, or to the same person over and over.
tldr.mechanism: The Sieve vacation action sends one reply to the sender's envelope address, remembers who has been answered for a number of days, and refuses to reply to list mail, automated mail and mail not addressed to the user.
tldr.outcome: It gives Sieve scripts a standard autoresponder with built-in safety rules. The base specification is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8580.

facts.label: Default :days
facts.value: 7, or the site minimum if greater

facts.label: Site maximum :days
facts.value: MUST be greater than 7, SHOULD be greater than 30

today: RFC 5230 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8580. It remains the definition of the Sieve vacation action.

sections.title: Introduction and Capability
sections.content:
RFC 5230 adds a vacation action to the Sieve email filtering language from RFC 5228. Its job is to tell correspondents that their messages will not be answered right away. It is modelled on the Unix vacation command.

A Sieve implementation that supports it advertises the capability identifier vacation, and scripts load it with require "vacation". The reply is always addressed to the Return-Path address (the envelope sender) of the message being answered.
sections.eli5: Sieve is a set of mail rules. This adds one new rule: 'send back a note saying I am away'. The note goes back to whoever sent the mail.

sections.title: The Vacation Action and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The action looks like this: vacation [":days" number] [":subject" string] [":from" string] [":addresses" string-list] [":mime"] [":handle" string] <reason: string>. Only the reason text is required.

  • :days sets how long a sender is remembered. The minimum is normally 1 (a site may raise it, but it must stay above 0). A site may set a maximum, which MUST be greater than 7 and SHOULD be greater than 30. If omitted, the default is 7 or the minimum, whichever is greater. Out-of-range values are clamped to the minimum or maximum.
  • :subject sets the reply subject. UTF-8 is allowed, and it MUST be converted to RFC 2047 encoded words if and only if non-ASCII characters are present.
  • :from sets an alternate From address. It must be a valid mailbox-list, and implementations SHOULD check the syntax. Values that fail a validity check are suggested to be ignored rather than make the action fail.
  • :mime says the reason string is a full MIME entity, headers included. Without it, the reason is a UTF-8 string.
  • :addresses and :handle are covered in the following sections.
sections.eli5: You can fill in a few blanks on the note: how many days before telling the same person again, what the title says, who it is from, and the message itself.

sections.title: Tracking Who Has Been Answered
sections.content:
Vacation keeps a record of the responses it has sent to each address during the :days period. If the same response was not sent to that address within the period, it is sent; otherwise it is skipped.

Tracking is per address and per response. A response is identified either by an explicit :handle name, or by the combination of :subject, :from, :mime and the reason text when no handle is given. So if a script sends different reasons for different incoming subjects, one sender can legitimately receive both. This behavior is REQUIRED.

There is one exception. If the variables extension (RFC 5229) is used, the arguments MUST NOT have undergone variable expansion before tracking. This stops a script like :subject "Automatic response to: ${1}" from replying to every message with a different subject line.

Giving two vacation actions the same :handle makes them count as one response, so the sender gets only a single reply. Implementations are free to limit how many responses they remember, but the limit MUST NOT be less than 1000, and the oldest SHOULD be discarded first. An implementation note suggests hashing counted or null-terminated strings, so that the same text used in different optional parameters cannot produce the same hash. Implementations MAY reset the records when a script changes.
sections.eli5: The robot keeps a list of who it already told and when. It will not tell the same person the same thing again until enough days have passed.

sections.title: When Not to Reply
sections.content:
Vacation MUST NOT respond unless the user's address appears in a To, Cc, Bcc, Resent-To, Resent-Cc or Resent-Bcc line. An address counts as the user's if the implementation knows it, if it is the final envelope recipient, or if the script lists it with :addresses.

Implementations MUST keep a list of addresses that vacation never writes to, though its contents are implementation defined. It is meant to cover system daemons. Suggested entries include MAILER-DAEMON, LISTSERV, majordomo, addresses ending in -request and addresses beginning with owner-. The RFC warns against blindly copying RFC 2142, because some addresses such as POSTMASTER are read by people who do care that the user is away.

Implementations SHOULD NOT respond to messages that carry a List-Id, List-Help, List-Subscribe, List-Unsubscribe, List-Post, List-Owner or List-Archive header, or an Auto-submitted header with a value other than no.
sections.eli5: The robot only answers mail that was really sent to you, and it stays quiet for mailing lists and other robots. Otherwise two robots could write to each other all day.

sections.title: How the Reply Is Built
sections.content:
Section 5 lists the fields of the generated message.

  • Envelope sender: SHOULD be <>, with NOTIFY=NEVER on the RCPT TO line if the NOTARY extension of RFC 3461 is available.
  • Date: SHOULD be when the response was generated, which may differ from delivery time.
  • Subject: the :subject value, or else Auto: followed by the original subject. If there is no original subject, a fixed one such as Automated reply SHOULD be used.
  • From: SHOULD be the script owner's address unless :from overrides it.
  • To: SHOULD be the recipient of the response.
  • Auto-Submitted: SHOULD be auto-replied.
  • In-Reply-To and References: In-Reply-To MUST be the original Message-ID and References SHOULD be updated with it, unless the original has no Message-ID.

The body is the reason string. Implementations MUST handle UTF-8 input. When :mime is used, headers must be 8-bit free, and implementations SHOULD reject vacation :mime actions containing 8bit header material.
sections.eli5: The reply is marked as automatic, comes from a blank return address so nobody can bounce an answer back at the robot, and points at the mail it answers.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Actions and Examples
sections.content:
Vacation does not change Sieve's implicit keep. It can run only once per script, and a script that tries to run two or more MUST fail with an error. It may be combined with discard, keep, fileinto and redirect, which is not an error, but it is incompatible with the reject and refuse actions.

The RFC's examples include a simple use with :days 23 and two extra addresses, and a script that redirects mail from the boss while sending everyone else a vacation reply. Section 7 shows scripts that choose the reply language from the Accept-Language or Content-Language header, or that use informal text for colleagues and formal text for outsiders. It also notes that :mime with multipart/alternative can carry several languages at once.
sections.eli5: You can only have one 'I am away' note per script. You can still have other rules that file or forward mail, and you can write different notes for different people or languages.

sections.title: Security and Standards Context
sections.content:
The RFC says it is critical that the restrictions are implemented correctly: replies MUST NOT be sent for messages not sent directly to the user, and MUST NOT be sent more often than :days allows unless the script changes. If mail is forwarded from a site that uses subaddressing, it may be impossible to list every recipient address with :addresses.

Vacation implements a 'Personal Responder' in the terminology of RFC 3834, and the RFC points to that document for the general security issues of autoresponders. It believes it adds no new ones. The extension is registered with IANA under the capability name vacation.
sections.eli5: The big danger is a robot that talks too much or to the wrong people. So the rules about who to answer and how often are strict.
